match.stem: The price of a notebook rises from Rs 50 to Rs 60, and the number of notebooks bought in a week by the students of a school falls from 200 to 150. Ignoring the sign, the price elasticity of demand for the notebook is:
match.explanation: Price elasticity of demand = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price), with both changes measured on the starting value. % change in quantity = (150 - 200) / 200 x 100 = -25%. % change in price = (60 - 50) / 50 x 100 = +20%. So eD = -25 / 20 = -1.25, and its absolute value is 1.25: demand is elastic. Taking the final values as the base gives 2.0, dividing the price change by the quantity change gives 0.8, and dividing the unit changes (50 / 10) gives 5.0.

match.stem: In a two-sector economy the consumption function is C = 60 + 0.75Y (in Rs crore). If investment rises from Rs 20 crore to Rs 40 crore, the new equilibrium level of income is:
match.explanation: At equilibrium Y = C + I = (60 + 0.75Y) + I, so Y(1 - 0.75) = 60 + I and Y = (autonomous consumption + I) / (1 - MPC). With the new investment I = 40: Y = (60 + 40) / 0.25 = 100 / 0.25 = Rs 400 crore. Rs 320 crore is the old equilibrium income (80 / 0.25, with I = 20), and Rs 80 crore is only the change in income (20 x multiplier 4), not its level. Rs 100 crore forgets to divide by (1 - MPC).

questions.stem: The aggregate value of goods and services produced in an economy can be calculated by three methods.

passage.title: GDP and Welfare
passage.text:
GDP is the sum total of the value of goods and services created within the geographical boundary of a country in a particular year. In order to compare the GDP figures and other macroeconomic variables of different countries or to compare the GDP figures of the same country at different points of time, we take the help of real GDP instead of relying on current market prices. The ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP gives us an idea of how prices have moved from the base year to the current year.  The Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Wholesale Price Index (WPI) are the other important ways to measure change of prices in an economy.

GDP gets distributed among the people as incomes and may treat higher level of GDP of a country as an index of greater well-being of the people of that country. But it may be incorrect to treat GDP as an index of the welfare of the country based on three reasons. Firstly, the distribution of GDP is not uniform, secondly, non-monetary exchanges are not accounted as part of economic activity and lastly, GDP does not take into account externalities.

questions.reason: accepted bank candidate computes the GDP deflator as nominal / real GDP x 100 from base-year and current-year price and quantity: same steps, new figures

match.stem: In the base year an economy produced 400 units of a good at Rs 15 per unit. In the current year it produced 500 units at Rs 24 per unit. The GDP deflator of the current year, in percentage terms, is:
match.explanation: GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP, and in percentage terms it is multiplied by 100. Nominal GDP of the current year = 500 x 24 = Rs 12,000. Real GDP of the current year at base-year prices = 500 x 15 = Rs 7,500. Deflator = 12,000 / 7,500 = 1.6, which is 160 per cent: prices are 1.6 times the base year (15 to 24). 1.6 forgets to multiply by 100, 62.5 turns the ratio upside down, and 200 divides by the base-year GDP (400 x 15 = 6,000), which wrongly counts the 25 per cent rise in output (400 to 500 units) as a rise in prices.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Wholesale Price Index (WPI) are the other important ways to measure change of prices in an economy.

GDP gets distributed among the people as incomes and may treat higher level of GDP of a country as an index of greater well-being of the people of that country. But it may be incorrect to treat GDP as an index of the welfare of the country based on three reasons. Firstly, the distribution of GDP is not uniform, secondly, non-monetary exchanges are not accounted as part of economic activity and lastly, GDP does not take into account externalities.

questions.stem: What is rural development?

passage.title: Rural Development
passage.text:
There is a greater need today to make rural areas more vibrant through diversification into dairying, poultry, fisheries, vegetables and fruits and linking up the rural production centres with the urban and foreign markets to realise higher returns on the investments in the products. Moreover, infrastructure elements like credit and marketing, farmer-friendly agricultural policies and a constant appraisal and dialogue between farmers' groups and state agricultural departments are essential to realise the full potential of the sector.

Today we cannot look at the environment and rural development as two distinct subjects. There is need to invent or procure alternate sets of eco-friendly technologies that lead to sustainable development in different circumstances such as organic farming. From these, each rural community can choose whatever will suit its purpose. We need to learn from, and also try out when found relevant, practices from the available set of 'best practice' illustrations to speed up this process of 'learning by doing'. A good example of such practice is creating a group and channelising their savings through micro credit whcih functions like mini banks for the development of agriculture.

options: A plan of action for the development of agricultural areas which are lagging behind in socio-economic development.
A plan of action for the development of rural areas which are lagging behind in socio-economic development.
A plan of action for the development of marginalised regions which are lagging behind in socio-economic and sustainable development indicators.
A plan of action for the development of urban which are lagging behind in socio-economic development
